result:
There is a particular hour, maybe seven in the evening, when the world exhales. The last hard light slants sideways through windows, the streets dimming slowly, and for a few minutes everything exists in that in-between space where neither day nor night owns the hour.

I return to this moment more often than I should. Not because it is special in any grand way, but because it is the one time the mind stops performing. During the day we narrate ourselves, rehearse conversations, catalog what to fix or finish or remember. But at this threshold the narration falters. The brain, having no clear task, simply watches. The sky changes color so slowly you can barely track it. A bird lands somewhere and shakes its head in a quick, mechanical jerk.

What strikes me is how little I see. The world is there, fully present, asking to be witnessed, and I am mostly thinking about dinner, or an email I forgot to send, or the way a sentence in a book I read last week had a rhythm I couldn't quite name. The actual evening — the purple bruise of the sky, the first cold thread of wind, the way distant cars look like small red and white teeth — passes through my awareness like water through an open hand.

And yet I keep coming back to this hour. Maybe because it is the closest we get to being a body that simply exists, before the night fills in and we start again.
